answers.turn_text: Oh man, what a terrible question, Rich. I go back and forth with this. It depends on my mood. My mood this morning is kind of optimistic. Sometimes I'm not optimistic. And it's such a toss-up that I think both of those interpretations fit. But I really see a lot of softness for Democrats in Maine and Michigan. And if I saw a single poll that had Mike Rogers on top, right now it's a 1.2 point race depending on the poll you look at. And Mike Rogers has not led in any major polls. So I'm inclined to say that it's El-Sayed's race to lose. But Rogers has momentum. El-Sayed doesn't. The conventional wisdom seems to be that Collins is in a better position than she was six years ago at least. If they lose one or both of those houses, they have no pathway really to the Senate majority because I don't think Iowa is going to flip necessarily. Texas and Alaska, Ohio and North Carolina are possible as a pathway even if Republicans manage to do better in the upper Midwest and Maine. But I think it's just such a 50-50. I'm going to say Democrats right now have the advantage. So 51%. But it's so close in all these states that it's too hard to render a verdict.
